items.stem: In AS English Language, what does the term ‘genre’ (text type) refer to?
options: The topic a text is about
A category of text recognised by shared conventions of form, purpose and language
items.answer: A category of text recognised by shared conventions of form, purpose and language
items.markingKey: Genre = a text type (speech, review, blog …) identified by its conventions.

items.stem: In Text B, an editorial in a national newspaper, ‘Pocket the Phones’, the writer includes ‘Schools should pocket the phones’. Explain how this is a convention of an editorial and why it suits the text’s purpose.
items.answer: It is a firm recommendation in the conclusion. It suits an editorial whose purpose is to argue that schools should ban phones, for adult newspaper readers, including parents and policymakers.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the convention (a firm recommendation in the conclusion); links it to the purpose (to argue that schools should ban phones); explains its effect on the audience (adult newspaper readers, including parents and policymakers).

items.stem: Explain why ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely.’ is typical of an information leaflet such as an information leaflet from a city transport department, ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely’.
items.answer: It is a clear, informative title. It suits an information leaflet whose purpose is to inform and instruct riders about safety rules, for members of the public who might hire e-scooters.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the convention (a clear, informative title); links it to the purpose (to inform and instruct riders about safety rules); explains its effect on the audience (members of the public who might hire e-scooters).

items.stem: Read Text B, a thread of comments posted under a local news website’s report on the Rialto closure. ‘@filmfan_88: Saw my first ever film there in 1996 😭 end of an era. | @nadia.k: Honestly? It was freezing and the sound was terrible. Nostalgia is fine but nobody actually WENT. | @filmfan_88: @nadia.k harsh but… fair 😂 | @localhistory: The Rialto opened in 1932 with a silent film and a live orchestra. Photos in our archive (link below). | @samuel_w: car park. a CAR PARK. unbelievable.’ Identify two conventions of an online comment thread in this extract. For each, quote the text and explain how it helps the writer achieve the purpose of the text.
items.answer: ‘@filmfan_88:’ – usernames that identify each contributor. ‘(link below)’ – hyperlinks to further material.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘@filmfan_88:’: usernames that identify each contributor; ‘(link below)’: hyperlinks to further material; explanation linked to purpose (to share personal reactions, memories and information).

items.stem: Read Text A, a feature article in a regional newspaper about the closure of the Rialto cinema. ‘For ninety-two years the Rialto has been the place where this town fell in love – with film stars, with stories, and quite often with each other. On Sunday its velvet curtains will close for the last time. Inside, the carpet is threadbare and the seats creak like old ships, but the projectionist, Mr Farouk, still climbs the narrow stairs each evening as he has done since 1979. “People say streaming killed us,” he shrugs. “Maybe. But you cannot laugh with three hundred strangers on your sofa.” The building will become a car park.’ Identify two conventions of a feature article in this extract. For each, quote the text and explain how it helps the writer achieve the purpose of the text.
items.answer: ‘For ninety-two years’ – an opening that establishes the history and human interest of the story. ‘the projectionist, Mr Farouk,’ – a named interviewee giving a human angle.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘For ninety-two years’: an opening that establishes the history and human interest of the story; ‘the projectionist, Mr Farouk,’: a named interviewee giving a human angle; ‘The building will become a car park.’: a pointed final sentence typical of a feature’s closing ‘kicker’; explanation linked to purpose (to inform readers of the closure and evoke nostalgia).

items.stem: Read Text A, a review from a city magazine’s food column. ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home. The new night market on Harbour Road is loud, cramped and gloriously chaotic, and I loved almost every minute. The star is a tiny stall run by two sisters who fold dumplings so fast their hands blur; their pork-and-chive parcels (six for a very reasonable price) are worth the twenty-minute queue alone. The grilled corn was a disappointment – charred outside, oddly cold within – and seating is a battle you will probably lose. Still, for sheer energy there is nothing like it in the city. Four stars.’ Analyse how the writer uses the conventions of a review, together with language and structure, to achieve the purpose of the text.
items.answer: Indicative content: a star rating giving an overall verdict; comment on value for money, which readers of reviews expect; balanced criticism alongside praise; ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home.’ (imperative): the playful commands address the reader directly and set a humorous, indulgent tone; ‘loud, cramped and gloriously chaotic’ (tricolon): two negative adjectives are turned positive by ‘gloriously’, showing the reviewer finds the chaos part of the charm; ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’ (hyperbole): the exaggeration creates a vivid image of skill and speed, making the stall seem like a spectacle; ‘charred outside, oddly cold within’ (antithesis): the balanced contrast gives a precise, concise criticism, showing the review is discriminating rather than gushing; register: informal, witty and evaluative.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO1 understanding and AO3 analysis of how meaning is shaped). Level 5 (9–10): insightful, sustained analysis of how a wide range of language features and structural choices shape meaning; precise, well-integrated quotation; perceptive about audience, purpose and context; fluent use of terminology; Level 4 (7–8): clear, developed analysis of a range of features with relevant quotation; effects explained in relation to audience and purpose; accurate terminology; Level 3 (5–6): some analysis of features with appropriate quotation; effects explained in general terms; some relevant terminology; Level 2 (3–4): identifies some features with limited comment on effect; some quotation; occasional terminology; Level 1 (1–2): mainly paraphrase or feature-spotting; little relevant comment on language. Indicative content: a star rating giving an overall verdict; comment on value for money, which readers of reviews expect; balanced criticism alongside praise; ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home.’ (imperative): the playful commands address the reader directly and set a humorous, indulgent tone; ‘loud, cramped and gloriously chaotic’ (tricolon): two negative adjectives are turned positive by ‘gloriously’, showing the reviewer finds the chaos part of the charm; ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’ (hyperbole): the exaggeration creates a vivid image of skill and speed, making the stall seem like a spectacle; ‘charred outside, oddly cold within’ (antithesis): the balanced contrast gives a precise, concise criticism, showing the review is discriminating rather than gushing; register: informal, witty and evaluative.

items.stem: Explain why ‘Pocket the Phones’ is typical of an editorial such as an editorial in a national newspaper, ‘Pocket the Phones’.
items.answer: It is a short, punchy imperative title that states the paper’s position. It suits an editorial whose purpose is to argue that schools should ban phones, for adult newspaper readers, including parents and policymakers.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks: 1 mark – identifies the convention (a short, punchy imperative title that states the paper’s position); 1 mark – links it to the purpose (to argue that schools should ban phones); 1 mark – explains its effect on the audience (adult newspaper readers, including parents and policymakers).

items.stem: Read Text B, a post from a personal running blog, ‘Kilometre 30’. ‘Nobody warns you about kilometre 30. The crowds have thinned, the energy gels taste like warm glue and your brain starts negotiating: just walk for a bit, nobody will know. I knew. At kilometre 31 a woman in a pink tutu overtook me, and something in me snapped – not my hamstring, thankfully, just my pride. I finished in 4 hours 12, which won’t trouble the record books, but I raised enough for half a ventilator. Next year, the whole thing. Tutu optional.’ Explain how the form, structure and language of this blog post would need to change if the same content were presented as a speech. Refer closely to the extract.
items.answer: It would need spoken signposting, direct address and a call to action; the register (informal, humorous and self-deprecating) and structure would change to suit the new form; specific phrases such as ‘Nobody warns you about kilometre 30.’ would be adapted.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: conventions of a speech: spoken signposting, direct address and a call to action; change of register from informal, humorous and self-deprecating; change of structure or layout; reference to a specific phrase that would change and why; awareness of how audience or purpose would shift.

items.stem: What is meant by the ‘context of production’ of a text?
options: The number of words it contains
The place where a reader happens to read it
The circumstances in which the text was created, such as who wrote it, when, where and why
items.answer: The circumstances in which the text was created, such as who wrote it, when, where and why
items.markingKey: Context of production = writer, time, place, publication and motive.

items.stem: Explain how ‘won’t trouble the record books’ helps a post from a personal running blog, ‘Kilometre 30’ achieve its purpose (to entertain and reflect on running a charity marathon).
items.answer: Understatement: the modest phrase plays down the achievement, creating a likeable persona.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark: 1 mark – names or describes the feature accurately (understatement, lexis and semantics).

items.stem: Explain how ‘together we will’ helps a speech by a city councillor at a residents’ meeting launching a rooftop-garden scheme achieve its purpose (to persuade residents to volunteer for the rooftop-garden scheme).
items.answer: Inclusive pronoun: ‘we’ unites councillor and residents as partners, reducing the sense of a politician giving orders.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks: 1 mark – names or describes the feature accurately (inclusive pronoun, pragmatics); 1 mark – explains the effect: ‘we’ unites councillor and residents as partners, reducing the sense of a politician giving orders.

items.stem: Leila is analysing a text. Read Text A, a speech by a city councillor at a residents’ meeting launching a rooftop-garden scheme. ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners – thank you for coming out on such a wet evening. Look up when you leave tonight. Every flat roof you see is a field waiting to be planted. Last summer, the pilot garden on the bus depot grew four hundred kilos of vegetables, cooled the building below by three degrees and gave thirty families somewhere to meet. Imagine that on every block. Some say it is too expensive. I say we cannot afford not to. So I am asking you tonight: lend us your hands, your weekends and your stubbornness, and together we will turn this grey city green.’ Identify the primary audience and give one piece of evidence.
items.answer: Local residents attending a public meeting; evidence such as ‘Some say it is too expensive. I say we cannot afford not to.’.
items.markingKey: 1 mark audience; 1 mark evidence [2]

items.stem: Ravi is analysing a text. Read Text B, a blog post by a resident, ‘My Year on the Roof’. ‘I’ll be honest: when the council asked for rooftop volunteers, I signed up mainly to get out of my flat. Twelve months later I have calloused hands, a slightly ridiculous number of chilli plants and – who knew? – actual friends. It isn’t all sunshine. The lift to the depot roof breaks constantly, the water tank leaked twice in August, and our tomatoes were demolished by pigeons. But on Saturday mornings, with the traffic grinding below and Mrs Okafor handing round her ginger tea, it feels like the only quiet place in the city. If you’re on the fence, come up and see. Bring gloves.’ (a) Identify the primary audience and give one piece of evidence. (b) State the main purpose of the text.
items.answer: (a) Other residents and general readers of a personal blog; evidence such as ‘It isn’t all sunshine.’. (b) To share a personal experience honestly and encourage others to join
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark audience; 1 mark evidence [2] (b) 1 mark: to share a personal experience honestly and encourage others to join [1]

items.stem: Read Text B, a blog post by a resident, ‘My Year on the Roof’. ‘I’ll be honest: when the council asked for rooftop volunteers, I signed up mainly to get out of my flat. But on Saturday mornings, with the traffic grinding below and Mrs Okafor handing round her ginger tea, it feels like the only quiet place in the city. If you’re on the fence, come up and see. Bring gloves.’ The text was written for other residents and general readers of a personal blog. Explain, with close reference to the text, what changes would be needed to adapt it for international visitors, and why.
items.answer: Changes: no local references or idioms, plain international English, practical details; specific phrases such as ‘I’ll be honest:’ and ‘If you’re on the fence, come up and see.’ would need adapting because the new audience has different needs and expectations.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: awareness of the new audience’s needs (no local references or idioms, plain international English, practical details); change to register or tenor; change to lexis, with an example from the text; change to structure, layout or length; change to purpose or emphasis; explanation of why each change suits the new audience.

items.stem: Kwame is analysing a text. Read Text A, an information leaflet from a city transport department, ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely’. ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely. E-scooters are now available to hire across the city centre. To keep yourself and others safe: • You must be 18 or over and hold a driving licence. • Ride on roads and cycle lanes only – never on pavements. • Wear a helmet. It could save your life. • Only one rider per scooter. Fines of up to $300 may be issued to riders who break these rules. For more information, visit our website or scan the QR code below.’ State the main purpose of the text.
items.answer: To inform and instruct riders about safety rules
items.markingKey: 1 mark: to inform and instruct riders about safety rules [1]

items.stem: In a transcript, what does the symbol (.) usually indicate?
options: A micropause of less than about half a second
items.answer: A micropause of less than about half a second
items.markingKey: Transcription key: (.) = micropause; (2) = a two-second pause.

items.stem: In a transcript, what does // usually indicate?
options: The point where speakers begin to overlap
items.answer: The point where speakers begin to overlap
items.markingKey: Overlapping speech is marked with // at the start of the overlap.

items.stem: Explain the function of ‘[Banner photograph: a line of hikers on a ridge at sunrise]’ in Text B, a page from a trekking company’s website.
items.answer: Image: the sunrise photograph suggests adventure, achievement and beauty before the reader reads a word.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark: 1 mark – names or describes the feature accurately (image, graphology and visual design).

items.stem: Read Text B, a page from a trekking company’s website. ‘[Banner photograph: a line of hikers on a ridge at sunrise] MONASTERY TRAIL – 5 DAYS | Moderate | From $640. Walk in the footsteps of pilgrims on one of the region’s most spectacular routes. ✔ Expert local guides ✔ Comfortable teahouse lodges ✔ All meals included. Day 3 is our favourite: you’ll climb above the clouds and watch eagles soar beneath your feet. “The best week of my life!” – Ana, Brazil [BOOK NOW button]’ Analyse two visual and verbal features in this text. Explain how the visual and written elements work together.
items.answer: ‘[Banner photograph: a line of hikers on a ridge at sunrise]’ – image: the sunrise photograph suggests adventure, achievement and beauty before the reader reads a word. ‘✔ Expert local guides ✔ Comfortable teahouse lodges ✔ All meals included’ – bullet points: the tick list reassures readers about safety and comfort at a glance.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘[Banner photograph: a line of hikers on a ridge at sunrise]’ (image): the sunrise photograph suggests adventure, achievement and beauty before the reader reads a word; ‘✔ Expert local guides ✔ Comfortable teahouse lodges ✔ All meals included’ (bullet points): the tick list reassures readers about safety and comfort at a glance; ‘Walk in the footsteps of pilgrims’ (imperative): the command invites the reader into the experience and gives the trek spiritual, historic significance; ‘you’ll climb above the clouds and watch eagles soar beneath your feet’ (direct address): second-person future tense lets readers imagine themselves on the trek, presenting it as certain and magical; ‘“The best week of my life!” – Ana, Brazil’ (testimonial): a customer’s exclamation provides social proof; naming her country suggests international appeal; ‘[BOOK NOW button]’ (interactive button): the capitalised button is a direct call to action that turns interest into a sale; ‘MONASTERY TRAIL – 5 DAYS | Moderate | From $640’ (compressed noun phrases): key facts are packed into a scannable line with no full sentences.

items.stem: Read Text B, a transcript of street interviews (vox pops) for a local news website; I is the interviewer, R1 and R2 are members of the public. (Transcription key: (.) micropause; (1) pause in seconds; // overlapping speech; CAPITALS = stressed word; [ ] non-verbal feature.) ‘I: what do you think of the new scooters R1: love them (.) honestly (.) I get to work in ten minutes instead of (.) what (.) forty on the bus I: and safety R1: well (.) I mean I’m careful (.) I don’t know about everyone else R2: they’re a menace (.) a MENACE (.) one nearly took my dog out yesterday (.) on the pavement I: on the pavement R2: on the pavement (.) and he just (.) laughed (.) went whizzing off’ Analyse how the speakers use language to express opinions and manage the interaction.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘love them’ (ellipsis): the subject ‘I’ is omitted, typical of quick, enthusiastic spoken replies; ‘instead of (.) what (.) forty’ (vague language): the self-directed ‘what’ and pause show the speaker estimating in real time; ‘well (.) I mean’ (discourse marker): the markers signal hesitation as the speaker moves to a less comfortable topic; ‘a menace (.) a MENACE’ (prosodic stress): the repetition with heavier stress intensifies R2’s anger; ‘took my dog out’ (idiom): the colloquial phrase exaggerates the near-miss vividly; ‘I: on the pavement’ (echoing): the interviewer repeats R2’s words to prompt more detail without asking a full question; ‘went whizzing off’ (onomatopoeia): the imitative ‘whizzing’ conveys the speed and carelessness of the rider; context: unscripted street interviews recorded and transcribed.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 8 (AO1 understanding and AO3 analysis of how meaning is shaped). Top level (6–8): insightful, sustained analysis of how a wide range of language features and structural choices shape meaning; precise, well-integrated quotation; perceptive about audience, purpose and context; fluent use of terminology; Middle level (4–5): some analysis of features with appropriate quotation; effects explained in general terms; some relevant terminology; Lower level (1–3): mainly paraphrase or feature-spotting; little relevant comment on language. I mean’ (discourse marker): the markers signal hesitation as the speaker moves to a less comfortable topic; ‘a menace (.) a MENACE’ (prosodic stress): the repetition with heavier stress intensifies R2’s anger; ‘took my dog out’ (idiom): the colloquial phrase exaggerates the near-miss vividly; ‘I: on the pavement’ (echoing): the interviewer repeats R2’s words to prompt more detail without asking a full question; ‘went whizzing off’ (onomatopoeia): the imitative ‘whizzing’ conveys the speed and carelessness of the rider; context: unscripted street interviews recorded and transcribed.

items.stem: In a comparative analysis, what is the most effective way to organise the answer?
options: Discuss only the text you prefer
Integrate the texts, comparing them point by point throughout
Write about Text A, then Text B, with no links
items.answer: Integrate the texts, comparing them point by point throughout
items.markingKey: Integrated comparison is rewarded more highly than writing about each text separately.

items.stem: Text A (a news article from a national newspaper) includes ‘Critics argue’. Text B (a transcript of a radio phone-in in which the presenter (P) talks to a caller (C)) includes ‘exactly (.) exactly that’. Compare how these quotations reflect the different forms and purposes of the two texts.
items.answer: Text A: concession – the reporting clause introduces an opposing view, giving balance and ending on an unresolved controversy. Text B: repetition – the repeated agreement shows the caller accepting the presenter’s summary. The difference reflects to inform readers about the water shortage and the new restrictions versus to air a listener’s complaint and entertain the audience with lively talk.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: feature/effect in Text A (concession); feature/effect in Text B (repetition); a comparative point linked to form or purpose (e.g. Text A is planned, formal written news with attributed quotation;. Text B is unplanned spoken interaction with fillers, pauses and overlaps).

items.stem: Text A (a speech by a city councillor at a residents’ meeting launching a rooftop-garden scheme) includes ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners’. Text B (a blog post by a resident, ‘My Year on the Roof’) includes ‘Bring gloves.’. Compare how these quotations reflect the different forms and purposes of the two texts.
items.answer: Text A: tricolon – the three-part address widens from personal to shared identity, flattering the audience as ‘gardeners’ before they have agreed to anything. Text B: minor sentence – the clipped final command is practical and witty, ending on an invitation rather than a lecture. The difference reflects to persuade residents to volunteer for the rooftop-garden scheme versus to share a personal experience honestly and encourage others to join.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: feature/effect in Text A (tricolon); feature/effect in Text B (minor sentence); a comparative point linked to form or purpose (e.g. Text A presents the scheme as a public cause through rousing rhetoric, while Text B offers a personal, humorous account that admits practical problems).

items.stem: Read Text A, a news article from a national newspaper. ‘Reservoirs at Record Low as Heatwave Grips Capital. Water levels in the capital’s three main reservoirs have fallen to 31 per cent of capacity, the lowest figure since records began in 1978, officials confirmed yesterday. From Monday, the use of hosepipes and sprinklers will be banned, and car washes must recycle at least half of the water they use. “We are not yet in a crisis,” said Dr Leila Haddad, director of the regional water authority, “but every household can make a difference.” Forecasters expect temperatures to remain above 38°C for at least another week. Critics argue that the authority has failed to repair leaking pipes, which lose an estimated fifth of all treated water.’ Read Text B, a transcript of a radio phone-in in which the presenter (P) talks to a caller (C). (Transcription key: (.) micropause; (1) pause in seconds; // overlapping speech; CAPITALS = stressed word; [ ] non-verbal feature.) ‘P: and on line two we’ve got Samuel (.) morning Samuel C: morning (.) erm yeah I just wanted to say (.) I’m sick of being told to take shorter showers when // P: // right C: when the pipes on my street have been leaking for (1) three MONTHS P: three months (.) wow C: yeah you can literally see it (.) bubbling up by the bus stop (.) and nobody’s come P: so you’d say the authority’s (.) passing the buck a bit C: exactly (.) exactly that (.) fix your own leaks first you know P: fair point (.) we have asked them on to the show (.) let’s see if they turn up [laughs]’ (a) Identify one similarity in the purpose of the two texts. (b) Explain one difference in form and its effect.
items.answer: (a) Both concern a water shortage during a heatwave; A aims to inform readers about the water shortage and the new restrictions, B aims to air a listener’s complaint and entertain the audience with lively talk. (b) Text A presents the authority’s view and the critics’ view in a balanced way; Text B focuses on one listener’s anger
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark similarity; 1 mark reference [2] (b) 1 mark difference; 1 mark effect [2]

items.stem: Read Text A, an extract from a travel memoir about trekking to a mountain monastery. ‘By the third day my legs had stopped complaining and simply given up. The path zigzagged above the cloud line, and every time I thought I had reached the top, another ridge rose ahead of me like a cruel joke. Our guide, Pema, walked as if the mountain were flat, humming to himself and pausing only to point out a vulture circling below us. Below us. I remember that more than anything: looking down at a bird in flight. When the monastery finally appeared, its prayer flags snapping in the wind, I did not feel triumph. I felt very small, and strangely grateful.’ Read Text B, a page from a trekking company’s website. ‘[Banner photograph: a line of hikers on a ridge at sunrise] MONASTERY TRAIL – 5 DAYS | Moderate | From $640. Walk in the footsteps of pilgrims on one of the region’s most spectacular routes. ✔ Expert local guides ✔ Comfortable teahouse lodges ✔ All meals included. Day 3 is our favourite: you’ll climb above the clouds and watch eagles soar beneath your feet. “The best week of my life!” – Ana, Brazil [BOOK NOW button]’ (a) Identify one similarity in the purpose of the two texts. (b) Compare the register of the two texts.
items.answer: (a) Both concern trekking to a mountain monastery; A aims to recount and reflect on a personal journey, and to entertain, B aims to persuade readers to book the trek. (b) A is literary, reflective and personal; B is enthusiastic, promotional and concise.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark similarity; 1 mark reference [2] (b) 1 mark each text; 1 mark comparative comment [3]

items.stem: Read Text B, a post from a personal running blog, ‘Kilometre 30’. ‘Nobody warns you about kilometre 30. The crowds have thinned, the energy gels taste like warm glue and your brain starts negotiating: just walk for a bit, nobody will know. I knew. At kilometre 31 a woman in a pink tutu overtook me, and something in me snapped – not my hamstring, thankfully, just my pride. I finished in 4 hours 12, which won’t trouble the record books, but I raised enough for half a ventilator. Next year, the whole thing. Tutu optional.’ Analyse the ways in which form, structure and language are used to engage readers of a personal blog, many of them runners.

items.stem: Read Text A, a feature article in a regional newspaper about the closure of the Rialto cinema. ‘For ninety-two years the Rialto has been the place where this town fell in love – with film stars, with stories, and quite often with each other. On Sunday its velvet curtains will close for the last time. Inside, the carpet is threadbare and the seats creak like old ships, but the projectionist, Mr Farouk, still climbs the narrow stairs each evening as he has done since 1979. “People say streaming killed us,” he shrugs. “Maybe. But you cannot laugh with three hundred strangers on your sofa.” The building will become a car park.’ What is the primary purpose of this text?
items.answer: To inform
items.markingKey: To inform: the text aims to inform readers of the closure and evoke nostalgia.

items.stem: Read Text A, a review from a city magazine’s food column. ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home. The grilled corn was a disappointment – charred outside, oddly cold within – and seating is a battle you will probably lose. Still, for sheer energy there is nothing like it in the city. Four stars.’ Read Text B, a promotional leaflet for the same night market. ‘HARBOUR ROAD NIGHT MARKET [image: strings of lanterns above crowded stalls] Taste the world in one street! Bring the whole family – kids eat free before 7 pm on Sundays! Find us: two minutes from Harbour Road station. Follow us @harbournights for this week’s specials.’ Identify one similarity in the purpose of the two texts.
items.answer: Both concern a night market; A aims to evaluate the market and entertain readers, B aims to persuade people to visit the market.

items.stem: Read Text A, a transcript from a student podcast in which two presenters, Kenji (K) and Zara (Z), discuss a new ban on phones in school. (Transcription key: (.) micropause; (1) pause in seconds; // overlapping speech; CAPITALS = stressed word; [ ] non-verbal feature.) ‘K: so (.) the ban (.) week one (.) how are we feeling Z: honestly (.) I thought I’d hate it but (.) lunch is actually (.) louder now (.) like people TALK K: [laughs] people talk (.) shocking Z: no but seriously // K: // I know I know Z: there was this one boy who was (.) he was just playing cards with the year sevens (.) which (.) never would have happened before K: mm (.) I do miss checking the bus times though (.) that’s a genuine (.) problem isn’t it Z: true (.) true (.) they could put a screen up in the canteen or something’ Analyse two features of spontaneous speech in this text. Comment on what they reveal about the relationship between the speakers.
items.answer: ‘so (.) the ban (.) week one’ – ellipsis: the verbless noun phrases sketch the topic quickly, typical of spontaneous speech, as listeners can infer the meaning. ‘honestly’ – discourse marker: signals a sincere, personal opinion and marks the start of Zara’s turn.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘so (.) the ban (.) week one’ (ellipsis): the verbless noun phrases sketch the topic quickly, typical of spontaneous speech, as listeners can infer the meaning; ‘honestly’ (discourse marker): signals a sincere, personal opinion and marks the start of Zara’s turn; ‘like people TALK’ (prosodic stress): the stress on ‘TALK’ highlights the surprising change and adds humour; ‘[laughs] people talk (.) shocking’ (irony): Kenji’s mock amazement gently teases the idea that talking is remarkable, building rapport through humour; ‘// I know I know’ (overlap): the overlapping reassurance shows cooperative, friendly talk rather than an attempt to take the floor; ‘who was (.) he was just’ (false start): the self-repair shows the speaker planning in real time; ‘that’s a genuine (.) problem isn’t it’ (tag question): the tag invites agreement, softening a criticism of the ban and passing the turn to Zara; ‘or something’ (vague language): the vague tag keeps the suggestion tentative and conversational.

items.stem: Read Text B, a transcript of a radio phone-in in which the presenter (P) talks to a caller (C). (Transcription key: (.) micropause; (1) pause in seconds; // overlapping speech; CAPITALS = stressed word; [ ] non-verbal feature.) ‘P: and on line two we’ve got Samuel (.) morning Samuel C: morning (.) erm yeah I just wanted to say (.) I’m sick of being told to take shorter showers when // P: // right C: when the pipes on my street have been leaking for (1) three MONTHS P: three months (.) wow C: yeah you can literally see it (.) bubbling up by the bus stop (.) and nobody’s come P: so you’d say the authority’s (.) passing the buck a bit C: exactly (.) exactly that (.) fix your own leaks first you know P: fair point (.) we have asked them on to the show (.) let’s see if they turn up [laughs]’ Analyse how the speakers use language to express opinions and manage the interaction.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘morning Samuel’ (phatic talk): the greeting builds friendly rapport and welcomes the caller on air rather than conveying information; ‘erm yeah I just wanted to say’ (filler): the filler and hedged opener show unplanned speech and the caller’s slight nervousness on air; ‘// right’ (overlap): the presenter’s overlapping ‘right’ is supportive back-channelling, encouraging the caller to continue; ‘three MONTHS’ (prosodic stress): the stressed word conveys the caller’s anger and makes the length of the delay the focus; ‘three months (.) wow’ (echoing): the presenter repeats the caller’s words to validate the complaint and emphasise it for listeners; ‘passing the buck a bit’ (reformulation): the presenter sums up the complaint in an idiom, framing it for listeners; ‘a bit’ softens the accusation; ‘exactly (.) exactly that’ (repetition): the repeated agreement shows the caller accepting the presenter’s summary; ‘[laughs]’ (implicature): the laugh implies doubt that the authority will appear, aligning the presenter with the caller without openly criticising; context: a live, unscripted local radio phone-in during the water restrictions.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO1 understanding and AO3 analysis of how meaning is shaped). Level 5 (9–10): insightful, sustained analysis of how a wide range of language features and structural choices shape meaning; precise, well-integrated quotation; perceptive about audience, purpose and context; fluent use of terminology; Level 4 (7–8): clear, developed analysis of a range of features with relevant quotation; effects explained in relation to audience and purpose; accurate terminology; Level 3 (5–6): some analysis of features with appropriate quotation; effects explained in general terms; some relevant terminology; Level 2 (3–4): identifies some features with limited comment on effect; some quotation; occasional terminology; Level 1 (1–2): mainly paraphrase or feature-spotting; little relevant comment on language. Indicative content: ‘morning Samuel’ (phatic talk): the greeting builds friendly rapport and welcomes the caller on air rather than conveying information; ‘erm yeah I just wanted to say’ (filler): the filler and hedged opener show unplanned speech and the caller’s slight nervousness on air; ‘// right’ (overlap): the presenter’s overlapping ‘right’ is supportive back-channelling, encouraging the caller to continue; ‘three MONTHS’ (prosodic stress): the stressed word conveys the caller’s anger and makes the length of the delay the focus; ‘three months (.) wow’ (echoing): the presenter repeats the caller’s words to validate the complaint and emphasise it for listeners; ‘passing the buck a bit’ (reformulation): the presenter sums up the complaint in an idiom, framing it for listeners; ‘a bit’ softens the accusation; ‘exactly (.) exactly that’ (repetition): the repeated agreement shows the caller accepting the presenter’s summary; ‘[laughs]’ (implicature): the laugh implies doubt that the authority will appear, aligning the presenter with the caller without openly criticising; context: a live, unscripted local radio phone-in during the water restrictions.

items.stem: Text A (a fundraising email from a children’s hospital charity) includes ‘costs less than a family car’. Text B (a post from a personal running blog, ‘Kilometre 30’) includes ‘taste like warm glue’. Compare how these quotations reflect the different forms and purposes of the two texts.
items.answer: Text A: precise numerical detail – the comparison makes an expensive item feel affordable and relatable. Text B: simile – the unpleasant comparison is comic and conveys physical misery. The difference reflects to persuade readers to sign up for a fundraising run versus to entertain and reflect on running a charity marathon.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: feature/effect in Text A (precise numerical detail); feature/effect in Text B (simile); a comparative point linked to form or purpose (e.g. Text A uses one child’s story and emotive lexis to make readers act;. Text B uses humour and self-deprecation to entertain).

items.stem: Text A (a news article from a national newspaper) includes ‘“We are not yet in a crisis,” said’. Text B (a transcript of a radio phone-in in which the presenter (P) talks to a caller (C)) includes ‘three months (.) wow’. Compare how these quotations reflect the different forms and purposes of the two texts.
items.answer: Text A: direct quotation – quoting a named expert adds credibility and balance, and the reassuring tone contrasts with the alarming figures. Text B: echoing – the presenter repeats the caller’s words to validate the complaint and emphasise it for listeners. The difference reflects to inform readers about the water shortage and the new restrictions versus to air a listener’s complaint and entertain the audience with lively talk.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: feature/effect in Text A (direct quotation); feature/effect in Text B (echoing); a comparative point linked to form or purpose (e.g. Text A is planned, formal written news with attributed quotation;. Text B is unplanned spoken interaction with fillers, pauses and overlaps).

items.stem: Read Text A, a fundraising email from a children’s hospital charity. ‘Dear Supporter, Six-year-old Mateo spent his last birthday in a hospital bed, wired to a machine that breathed for him. Today he is learning to ride a bike. The difference? A specialist ventilator, bought with money raised by runners like you. This year we need forty more ventilators. Each one costs less than a family car, yet each one gives a child back their future. Will you run for Mateo on 12 March? Sign up today, and we will send you a free training plan and your charity vest. With heartfelt thanks, The Fundraising Team’ Read Text B, a post from a personal running blog, ‘Kilometre 30’. ‘Nobody warns you about kilometre 30. The crowds have thinned, the energy gels taste like warm glue and your brain starts negotiating: just walk for a bit, nobody will know. I knew. At kilometre 31 a woman in a pink tutu overtook me, and something in me snapped – not my hamstring, thankfully, just my pride. I finished in 4 hours 12, which won’t trouble the record books, but I raised enough for half a ventilator. Next year, the whole thing. Tutu optional.’ Identify one similarity in the purpose of the two texts.
items.answer: Both concern running a marathon for charity; A aims to persuade readers to sign up for a fundraising run, B aims to entertain and reflect on running a charity marathon.
items.markingKey: 1 mark similarity; 1 mark reference [2]

items.stem: Read Text A, an information leaflet from a city transport department, ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely’. ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely. E-scooters are now available to hire across the city centre. To keep yourself and others safe: • You must be 18 or over and hold a driving licence. • Ride on roads and cycle lanes only – never on pavements. • Wear a helmet. It could save your life. • Only one rider per scooter. Fines of up to $300 may be issued to riders who break these rules. For more information, visit our website or scan the QR code below.’ Identify two conventions of an information leaflet in this extract. For each, quote the text and explain how it helps the writer achieve the purpose of the text.
items.answer: ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely.’ – a clear, informative title. ‘• Only one rider per scooter.’ – rules presented as a bulleted list.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Riding an E-scooter Safely.’: a clear, informative title; ‘• Only one rider per scooter.’: rules presented as a bulleted list; ‘For more information, visit our website’: signposting to further information; explanation linked to purpose (to inform and instruct riders about safety rules); or any other valid, supported point.

items.stem: Text A is a feature article in a regional newspaper about the closure of the Rialto cinema; Text B is a thread of comments posted under a local news website’s report on the Rialto closure, both on the closure of an old cinema. From Text A: (i) ‘the seats creak like old ships’ (ii) ‘its velvet curtains will close for the last time’. From Text B: (iii) ‘end of an era’ (iv) ‘Photos in our archive (link below).’. Using these quotations, compare the two texts, focusing on how each writer conveys attitude.
items.answer: ‘the seats creak like old ships’: simile – the comparison suggests age and romance, making decline seem dignified. ‘its velvet curtains will close for the last time’: metaphor – the closing curtains symbolise the end of an era, giving the closure theatrical finality. ‘end of an era’: cliché – the familiar phrase sums up the loss quickly, typical of informal online comment. ‘Photos in our archive (link below).’: compressed noun phrases – the verbless phrasing and link are typical of informative online posts. Overall: Text A is a single, crafted journalistic voice; Text B is many short, informal voices responding to each other.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘the seats creak like old ships’ – simile: the comparison suggests age and romance, making decline seem dignified; ‘its velvet curtains will close for the last time’ – metaphor: the closing curtains symbolise the end of an era, giving the closure theatrical finality; ‘end of an era’ – cliché: the familiar phrase sums up the loss quickly, typical of informal online comment; ‘Photos in our archive (link below).’ – compressed noun phrases: the verbless phrasing and link are typical of informative online posts; a comparative judgement, e.g. Text A is a single, crafted journalistic voice; Text B is many short, informal voices responding to each other. At least one mark must come from an explicit comparison.
